definition.body: Implicit memory is the human-made cognitive category for memory systems that operate without conscious awareness, intentional recall, or deliberate retrieval. Parameters: (1) content — information stored and expressed through performance rather than conscious recollection, including motor skills, perceptual priming, classical conditioning, and non-associative learning; (2) expression — the stored influence manifests as improved performance, faster response times, or altered behavior without the subject's awareness of the source; (3) consciousness boundary — unlike declarative memory, implicit memory does not require or produce conscious access to the encoded content, though awareness of the task being performed may be present. It persists as a maintained classification in cognitive psychology textbooks, experimental paradigms (word-fragment completion, priming tasks, skin-conductance conditioning), and clinical neuropsychology for dissociating amnesic from intact memory systems. e.g.: the word-fragment priming paradigm in cognitive psychology experiments; motor skill retention in patients with hippocampal amnesia per the Mirror Drawing Task study by Squire and Zola-Morgan; classical conditioning of eye-blink response in Clark, Squire, and Steriade; the distinction between implicit and explicit memory in Schacter and Wagner's annual review of psychology | not: declarative-memory (conscious, intentionally retrievable memory); episodic-memory (conscious recall of personal events; a subtype of declarative not implicit) [formal: memoria implicita | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Inverse Short-Time Fourier Transform (ISTFT) is a signal-processing algorithm that reconstructs a time-domain signal from its short-time Fourier transform representation. Parameters: (1) window type — the analysis window function originally applied during STFT; (2) window size — the segment length in samples matching the original STFT; (3) hop size — the step between consecutive STFT frames; (4) window overlap — how consecutive segments are combined via overlap-add. The algorithm computes the inverse DFT of each frequency-bin segment, applies the inverse of the analysis window, and sums overlapping segments. definition.body: A gabor transform is a time-frequency analysis method that applies a sliding Gaussian window to a signal, computing the Fourier transform within each window position to produce a joint time-frequency representation. Unlike the generic STFT which permits arbitrary windows, the Gabor transform uses a symmetric Gaussian window function, which minimizes the Heisenberg-Gabor uncertainty product and yields the sharpest possible joint localization in time and frequency. Parameters: (1) the window width sigma, which sets the trade-off between time and frequency resolution; (2) the sampling grid in the time-frequency plane, specified as a time step and frequency step; (3) the window position sequence, which may be uniformly spaced or non-uniform. definition.body: The inverse Fourier transform is a human-made mathematical operation that reconstructs a time-domain function or discrete sequence from its frequency-domain representation. It applies an integral kernel e^(+jωt) to the complex-valued spectrum, summing sinusoidal components weighted by their frequency coefficients to recover the original signal. For the continuous case, the inverse Fourier transform computes f(t) = (1/2π) ∫_{-∞}^{∞} F(ω) e^(+jωt) dω; for the discrete case (IDFT), it computes x[n] = (1/N) Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k] e^(+j2πkn/N) for n=0,...,N-1. Parameters: (1) the input spectrum (complex-valued function of frequency), (2) the domain type (continuous-time, discrete-time, or discrete). Persistence mechanism: implemented as a core routine in numerical libraries (NumPy, SciPy, MATLAB ifft), embedded in DSP hardware for signal reconstruction, and taught as a fundamental operation in engineering and mathematics curricula. e.g.: inverse discrete Fourier transform in NumPy's numpy.fft.ifft function; inverse Fourier transform as the synthesis step in the textbook Signals and Systems by Oppenheim and Willsky; reconstruction of time-domain audio from spectral coefficients in the ISO/IEC 13818-3 MP3 decoder standard | not: the inverse short-time Fourier transform (which adds windowing and overlap-add); the discrete cosine transform (a different orthogonal transform used for lossy compression) [formal: transform Fourier inversa | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: A quadratic time-frequency representation that maps signal energy onto the time-frequency plane with exact marginal properties.

definition.body: The Wigner-Ville distribution is a human-made quadratic time-frequency representation that maps a signal onto the time-frequency plane by computing the bilinear product of the signal with its conjugate time-shift, then Fourier transforming with respect to the lag variable. Unlike linear time-frequency methods such as the short-time Fourier transform, the Wigner-Ville distribution achieves maximal joint time-frequency resolution and satisfies exact marginal properties: integrating over frequency yields instantaneous signal energy |s(t)|^2, and integrating over time yields the power spectral density |S(f)|^2. Its principal defect is cross-term interference: for a signal composed of multiple components, the distribution generates oscillating artifacts between each pair of components, making interpretation ambiguous for multicomponent signals. Parameters: (1) the input signal (real-valued, complex-valued, or discrete), (2) the analysis window (for smoothed variants such as the spectrogram or Born-Jordan distribution), (3) the lag window or kernel that controls cross-term suppression. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a core routine in signal analysis software and scientific computing libraries, documented as a standard method in time-frequency analysis textbooks, and applied in radar signal processing, vibration analysis, and quantum phase-space methods. e.g.: Wigner-Ville distribution in Boashash Time-Frequency Signal Analysis (2nd ed.); WVDA algorithm in MATLAB wavelet toolbox; instantaneous frequency estimation via WV marginals in radar chirp detection | not: the short-time Fourier transform (a linear time-frequency method); the spectrogram (the squared magnitude of the STFT) [formal: Wigner-Ville distribution | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cross-spectrum
payload.scope: A spectral representation quantifying the frequency-domain relationship between two signals, computed as the conjugate product of their individual spectra.

definition.body: The cross-spectrum is a human-made spectral representation that quantifies the frequency-domain relationship between two different signals. It is computed as the product of the complex conjugate of one signal spectrum with the spectrum of another signal: S_xy(f) = X*(f) * Y(f) where X and Y are the Fourier transforms of the two signals. Unlike the power spectrum which describes a single signal energy distribution, the cross-spectrum captures phase relationships and amplitude ratios between signals as functions of frequency. Key properties include: Hermitian symmetry (S_xy(f) = S_yx*(f)), linearity in each argument, and the ability to compute cross-correlation via inverse Fourier transform. Used to estimate transfer functions, coherence functions, and in adaptive filtering. Parameters: (1) the first signal (reference), (2) the second signal, (3) the spectral estimation method (direct DFT, averaged periodogram, or parametric). Persistence mechanism: implemented in signal analysis software and spectral estimation toolboxes, documented in standard textbooks on spectral analysis and signal processing, and applied in system identification, adaptive filtering, and array signal processing. e.g.: cross-spectrum analysis in Oppenheim and Schafer Digital Signal Processing (3rd ed.); cross-spectrum estimation in MATLAB pwelch function with two inputs; cross-spectral density computation in vibration analysis using BK PULSE software | not: power-spectrum (magnitude squared of a single signal FT, not cross-signal); coherence-function (normalized cross-spectrum magnitude, 0 to 1) [formal: spectrum inter-signale | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]
